items.abstract:
<jats:p>
            Tropek
            <jats:italic>et al</jats:italic>
            . critique the Hansen
            <jats:italic>et al</jats:italic>
            . global forest loss paper in terms of its utility and accuracy. Both criticisms suffer from a miscomprehension of the definition of forest employed as well as the requirements of product validation. Utility of the product is enhanced through its integration with forest type, carbon stock, protected area status, and other ancillary data.
          </jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Hansen
                    <jats:italic>et al</jats:italic>
                    . (Reports, 15 November 2013, p. 850) published a high-resolution global forest map with detailed information on local forest loss and gain. We show that their product does not distinguish tropical forests from plantations and even herbaceous crops, which leads to a substantial underestimate of forest loss and compromises its value for local policy decisions.
                  </jats:p>

items.abstract:
<jats:title>Forests in Flux</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Forests worldwide are in a state of flux, with accelerating losses in some regions and gains in others.
                    <jats:bold>
                      Hansen
                      <jats:italic>et al.</jats:italic>
                    </jats:bold>
                    (p.
                    <jats:related-article xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="doi" issue="6160" page="850" related-article-type="in-this-issue" vol="342" xlink:href="10.1126/science.1244693">850</jats:related-article>
                    ) examined global Landsat data at a 30-meter spatial resolution to characterize forest extent, loss, and gain from 2000 to 2012. Globally, 2.3 million square kilometers of forest were lost during the 12-year study period and 0.8 million square kilometers of new forest were gained. The tropics exhibited both the greatest losses and the greatest gains (through regrowth and plantation), with losses outstripping gains.
                  </jats:p>
